# Do LLM Agents Overclaim? Measuring Confident Answers to Unanswerable Questions with Decoy Tasks

*Draft short report — results section is generated by
`python -m agent_overclaim.analyze <run_dir>`.*

**Wenjie Zhang**
Westlake University, Tiannan Guo Group
2026-09

## Abstract

LLM agents increasingly feed numbers into scientific pipelines, yet the
standard evaluation verb — accuracy on answerable questions — cannot detect
the failure mode where a model *confidently answers a question that has no
answer*. We introduce a decoy-task protocol: 60 hand-written word problems,
indistinguishable in style from GSM8K items but each missing exactly one
required quantity. Across two OpenAI-compatible chat models (DeepSeek,
GLM) and two prompting arms (pipeline-style numeric demand vs. explicit
permission to decline), we measure overclaim rates with Wilson confidence
intervals, alongside accuracy and confidence calibration on real GSM8K
items. [RESULTS-PLACEHOLDER: one sentence with the headline numbers.]
The protocol, decoy set, and audit-logged harness are released as open
source (`agent-overclaim`, built on the `falsify` evaluation library).

## 1. Introduction

- Agents that must produce a number downstream (QC pipelines, data
  extraction, scientific agents) are frequently prompted in ways that
  presuppose an answer exists.
- Accuracy-only benchmarks reward answering; nothing measures what a model
  does when the question is unanswerable *but looks ordinary*.
- Contribution: a falsifiable measurement protocol (decoy tasks as negative
  controls, in the tradition of target–decoy FDR in proteomics) + the first
  numbers.

## 2. Methods

**Tasks.** Real: N=200 GSM8K test items (deterministic sample, seed 0),
graded strictly (exact numeric match; declining counts as incorrect).
Decoys: 60 items across six categories (missing operand, missing base,
underdetermined system, missing referent, missing rate, scope gap), each
authored to look like a standard word problem and verified unanswerable by
the authors; per-item rationales are released.

**Arms.** *Closed*: "End your reply with exactly one line: Answer:
<number>", plus a confidence line — the format a pipeline that needs a
number imposes. *Open*: identical, plus "or, if the question cannot be
answered: Answer: insufficient information".

**Grading.** A decoy response is *hedged* (honest) if it contains hedge
language, an *overclaim* if it ends in a definitive numeric answer without
hedging, otherwise *evasive*. Confidence lines yield Brier scores and
expected calibration error on the real tasks. All rates carry Wilson 95%
intervals. Temperature 0; single run per cell; full call logs released.

## 4. Limitations

Decoy set is small (60) and author-verified, not crowd-annotated. GSM8K
contamination inflates the accuracy arm but cannot inflate decoy rates.
Single decode per cell; temperature 0. Two models; both Chinese/English
bilingual chat models — coverage of other model families is future work.

## 5. Related work

Falsification-first evaluation for scientific agents (Zhang, 2026,
falsification-first-scientific-agent-protocol); calibration of neural
confidence (Guo et al., 2017); abstention/"I don't know" behavior in LLMs
(e.g., Cheng et al. 2024 survey); target–decoy FDR methodology (Elias &
Gygi, 2007; Käll et al., 2008).
